name: Rive
tagline: Editor and cross-platform runtimes for interactive vector animations with state machines, embedded in real apps and games.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Rive is two products welded together: a design tool for vector animation with state machines, and a set of hand-maintained runtimes that play the same .riv file identically on web, iOS, Android, Flutter, React Native and Unity. An agent can absolutely build you a keyframe editor that spits out JSON and a canvas player for the web, and that is a fun weekend. What it cannot do in a session is a production vector renderer with correct stroke joins, gradients, clipping and bones, plus a state machine engine, plus five platform ports that stay pixel-identical. The moment your animation has to ship inside a real mobile app, the runtime is the whole product and your JSON player is a demo. Build the toy if you enjoy it, but do not plan to migrate anything.
coreLoopDIY: A local browser tool where you draw simple vector shapes, keyframe their transforms and colors on a timeline, export a JSON file, and play it back with a tiny embeddable canvas runtime.
requirements: willingness to hand-author shapes if the drawing tools stay crude
a web-only target, since mobile runtimes are out of scope
whatYouLose: Runtimes for iOS, Android, Flutter, React Native and Unity that render the same file the same way
The real vector renderer: gradients, clipping, correct strokes, meshes, bones, constraints
State machines with inputs, listeners and blended transitions that designers can wire without a developer
Collaborative editing and a shared file format that designers and engineers actually hand back and forth
Years of edge-case polish in playback timing, scaling and layout fit modes
moatNotes: The .riv file is worthless without the runtimes, and the runtimes are worthless without the editor. Owning both ends is the business.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the alternative is paying an engineer to reimplement animation logic by hand in every platform your app ships on, and then maintaining it. Rive sells the handoff: a designer changes a transition, the file drops into the app, every platform agrees on what it looks like. That is not a feature you can clone, it is a maintenance burden someone else already carries. Teams pay to not own a renderer.
notes: A JSON timeline player is a weekend; a renderer that agrees with itself on six platforms is not. The moat is the runtime fleet plus the file format that only those runtimes can read.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user vector keyframe animation tool and a tiny playback runtime. Web only. No accounts, no backend, no telemetry, no cloud storage.

Stack, no substitutions: Vite + React + TypeScript, Zustand for state, plain HTML canvas 2D for rendering, no animation libraries.

Structure the repo as two packages in one folder: /editor (the app) and /runtime (a dependency-free ~300 line TS module that takes a document JSON plus a canvas and plays it).

Document model, define it as a TS type shared by both packages:
- document: width, height, fps, duration, shapes[], tracks[]
- shape: id, type of rect | ellipse | path (path = array of cubic segments), fill color, stroke color, stroke width, transform (x, y, rotation, scaleX, scaleY, opacity), parentId for nesting
- track: shapeId, property name, keyframes[] of { frame, value, easing of linear | easeIn | easeOut | easeInOut }

Editor requirements:
- Canvas viewport with pan and zoom, click to select, drag to move, handles to scale and rotate
- Tool buttons to add rect, ellipse and a 4-point editable path
- Left panel: shape tree with drag to reparent, rename, delete
- Right panel: numeric inputs for the selected shape's transform, fill, stroke
- Bottom timeline: one row per animated property, keyframe diamonds you can drag, a scrubber, play/pause/loop, frame stepping
- Setting a property value while the playhead is on a frame creates or updates a keyframe on that frame
- Interpolation: numbers lerp with the chosen easing, colors lerp in sRGB, rotations shortest path
- File menu: New, Open (File System Access API with an input[type=file] fallback), Save As .json, Export current frame as PNG

Runtime requirements:
- createPlayer(canvas, doc) returning play, pause, seek(frame), setLoop(bool), destroy
- Fit modes: contain, cover, fill
- requestAnimationFrame loop driven by wall clock, not frame counting, so playback speed is correct on any display
- Zero imports from /editor

Also ship /demo/index.html that loads a bundled sample .json through the runtime with no editor code, to prove the split works.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: state machines, bones or meshes, gradients, boolean ops, text, image fills, mobile or native runtimes, real time collaboration, plugin systems.

Write a README with run instructions, the document JSON schema, and a blunt Limitations section listing everything in the out of scope list. Add Vitest unit tests for the interpolation math and for keyframe insert/update/delete.
